title: Monday, sixty tickets
setting: A team lead divides the weekend's queue between four people.

lines.t: Sixty in the ticket queue and four of us. We triage before anyone starts answering.
Half of them are marked high priority.
Priority level is what the user feels. Severity is what it does to the business.
So the warehouse being offline beats one broken mouse.
Assign that ticket to yourself and start now.
What about the service level agreement? We're at three hours on some of these.
The agreement gives us four hours to respond. Respond, not solve.
Ticket 9101 is back. Same person, same error, closed on Friday.
Someone closed it too early. Reopen the ticket and escalate to second line.
Doing it now. And I'll call him myself, so he doesn't hear it from the system.

title: Nobody else can see it
setting: Two engineers work out why a fault appears for three people and nobody else.

lines.t: I can't replicate the issue. It works every time on my machine.
How many affected users?
Three. All in the Burgas office, all before nine in the morning.
That narrows it down more than anything else in the ticket.
The symptom is the same every time. The page loads, then goes blank.
Do we have an error code?
Only one of them wrote it down. E dash five zero three.
So it's intermittent and the time of day is the pattern. Ask them for the steps to reproduce before they start work tomorrow.
You think it's the backup again?
Maybe. We isolate the cause by turning one thing off at a time, and we start with whatever runs at 08:45.

title: Before you reinstall anything
setting: A user calls the helpdesk because the accounting program keeps closing itself.

lines.t: Good morning. The accounting program won't open. It just closes again.
Let's see why. Does anything appear on the screen before it closes?
A grey box with numbers. I clicked it away.
Next time read me the code before you close it, including the letters.
It's back. E dash four zero one one.
Thank you. Bear with me while I check that code.
Should I reinstall it? A colleague told me to reinstall it.
Hold on. Log out and back in first. That clears this one more often than it should.
It's open. I feel a bit silly now.
Twenty people a month hit this. I'm documenting the fix so the next one gets an answer in a minute.

title: Her first day from home
setting: Support helps a colleague who cannot get into anything on her first day working from home.

lines.t: It's my first day working from home and I can't get into anything.
I'll walk you through it step by step. None of it is difficult.
The login screen says my password is wrong.
I'm doing a password reset now. You'll get a text in about ten seconds.
That worked. But the printer still isn't there.
Can you screen share, or shall I start a remote session?
I don't know how to screen share.
Then I'll take the remote session. You'll see the mouse moving on its own, and that's me.
There's a yellow triangle on the printer now.
Old driver. I'll reinstall it, then power cycle the printer: off, thirty seconds, on. If anything looks strange later, log out and back in before you call me.

title: Write it for Nina
setting: An engineer asks a colleague to check the message he is about to send to the whole company.

lines.t: Can you read this before I send it to everyone? Two minutes.
'We are deprecating the legacy VPN client ahead of the migration window.' What does that mean?
The old VPN stops working on Friday. Everyone installs the new one.
Then write that. What you've got is jargon from the first word.
It's accurate, though.
Accurate and useless. Your end user is Nina in accounts, not another engineer.
All right. How would you break it down?
Three lines. What changes, when it happens, and what they have to do. In plain English.
Let me rephrase it and send it back to you.
Do that. And check understanding before Friday. Ask two non-technical people to tell you what they'll have to do.

title: Since eight this morning
setting: A customer has been waiting all day for the order system to come back.

lines.t: Your order system has been down since eight this morning. Eight.
I apologise for the inconvenience. Bear with me while I open your account.
I've been told 'bear with me' four times today.
Then I'll say something useful instead. It's with the supplier and I'm going to chase them up now, while you stay on the line.
Go on, then.
They have an engineer on it. He says two hours.
Two hours is what they said at ten o'clock.
I'll look into what changed and give you a progress update at one, whether there's news or not.
And if there isn't?
Then I put it in writing, with all the times, and you take that to whoever you need to.

title: Fourth time this month
setting: An agent hands a repeat problem to the team lead at shift handover.

lines.t: Ticket 8842. The Varna office lost the shared drive again this morning.
Again? How many is that now?
Fourth time this month. Same three users, always before nine.
Then it's a recurring issue, and we've been treating it as four separate ones.
I gave them the temporary fix. They map the drive by hand and carry on.
Good for this morning. Write it in the notes as a workaround, then escalate to second line.
Do I attach all four tickets?
All four. One ticket looks like bad luck. Four looks like a cause.
What goes in the internal note?
Times, usernames, and what you already tried. Then give the users a progress update at eleven, even if nothing has changed.

title: The lid and the meeting room
setting: A laptop comes back from the workshop for the third time with nothing wrong with it.

lines.t: The laptop from reception is back. Third visit, and the workshop says no fault found again.
Three visits and a healthy machine. What does she actually do when it happens?
Closes the lid, walks to the meeting room, opens it. Black screen.
Nobody tested that, because nobody walked anywhere.
Someone wrote 'user error' in the notes on the second visit.
Take it out. This is a recurring issue and we've marked it as resolved three times.
I gave her a temporary fix. She restarts it when she gets to the room.
Which she'll still be doing in a year unless someone finishes the job.
So where's the permanent fix?
In whatever happens to that machine between two rooms. And don't mark it as resolved until she says it's fine, not the workshop.

title: Two weeks off
setting: An engineer hands over his open tickets before going on holiday.

lines.t: I'm off for two weeks from Friday. What do you need from me?
The three tickets you're holding. Who do I pass them on to?
Two go to Martin. The third needs someone who knows the old payroll system.
That's nobody, which is why it's still open.
I'll document the fix I used last time. Four steps, and one of them makes no sense.
Put that one in an internal note with the reason. Otherwise somebody skips it.
Does the customer see any of this?
The internal note is for us. The write-up they get is three lines: what happened, what we did, what to do if it comes back.
And the changes I made on the server?
The audit trail has them, but it won't say why. Write the why down while you still remember it, then go and enjoy your holiday.
